newsitem.title: UK: Japanese bond yields may sink to new lows.
newsitem.headline: Japanese bond yields may sink to new lows.

text.p: Long-term Japanese bond yields could sink to fresh record lows of around two percent but strategists on Wednesday were nevertheless reluctant to recommend the paper, saying current levels were unsustainable.

The 182nd Japanese Government Bond (JGB) due 2005 made a record closing low yield of 2.180 percent on Wednesday after the bank of Japan's key "Tankan" survey was seen as leaving policy makers with little room to tighten credit.
"JGB yields can go lower, but it's an overshoot," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond stratgist at Nomura International in London.
"I don't see yields that low sustainable. It's simply a reaction to the lack of strength in the Tankan. There's very little fundamental reason for foreigners to be buying JGBs."
The key index in the quarterly Tankan that measures the mood of major manufacturers improved to plus two in March from minus three last November, at the higher end of economists' expectations.
This contrasted sharply with the mood in non-manufacturers, whose index plunged beyond most expectations to minus six from zero in November.
"I don't see the Bank of Japan raising interest rates until the first quarter 1998 -- this Tankan makes them even more likely to hold off until then," said Gibbs.
The key 10-year JGB future was at 126.59 by mid-morning, down from 126.62 at the Tokyo close and off a contract high of 126.92 earlier in the session. The 10-year yield was at 2.170.
Strategists said the the long end of the Japanese curve would be underpinned by a benign interest rate outlook, expected yen appreciation and the use of JGBs as a diversification play in portfolios.
"It may not be surprising to see two percent 10-year yields if the yen tries to strengthen," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International here.
"But I'm still not recommending a buy strategy. JGB's don't favour any major long-term strategy."
Shah said the dollar/yen rate would reach 120 in the coming days. The dollar was at 122.38 yen in European trade and it has been falling from above 124.00 last week.

Analysts said the yen could retain a firm tone as the market focused on U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's planned meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Tokyo on Friday. Rubin is expected to talk tough with Japan on trade.
"For domestic investors it may be worthwhile chasing the rally, but for new investors, it's too late to invest in JGBs now unless you're very, very positive on the yen," said Shah.
Sean Shepley, international economist at Credit Suisse First Boston here, agreed the main reason for buying JGBs was the currency view with meagre yields doing little to tempt buyers.

"A lot of the big international funds are very heavily underweight JGBs," he said. "They do hold a lot of cash at the moment and there is this question about starting to rebalance being underweight JGBs, but clearly the market is making it rather difficult for them."
Gibbs said the next focus for the Japanese government bond market would be the round of asset allocation decisions for the new fiscal year, usually determined around mid to late April.
"A lot of attention will be paid to the relative shifts in allocation between domestic and foreign holdings," she said.
Analysts said foreign investors in JGBs should head for the mid-section of the curve.

"For a strategic play, if you're holding the shorter end, say two to four years, you may want to move to the five to six years, because most of the curve flattening will happen at the short end," said Gibbs.
Shah also favoured the five year sector, adding that although the curve would flatten near term, there would likely be some steepening in the medium to longer term.
